transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Morales (CTO - AtlasPay), Tom Becker (ML Infra Lead), Priya Singh (SRE)

Summary (auto): Quick context on AtlasPay's use case (fraud detection & transaction enrichment). Deep dive into runtime behavior for tool/function calling with structured JSON outputs; tradeoffs for constrained decoding, KV cache hits, batching windows, and quantization choices. Discussed Dedicated vs Private deployment impacts (VPC, KMS, egress). Action items and benchmarks agreed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Sofia from Redwood, with Ravi SE, and we are here to dig into the runtime side of tool calling and JSON constrained decoding like you requested.
[00:14] Lena Morales: Thanks, Sofia. We want to understand overheads when we push structured outputs (JSON) and how it affects latency and throughput. Our SLAs are pretty strict for enrichment -- tail latency under 300ms ideally.
[00:30] Ravi Patel: Great. Quick agenda: 1) show where overheads come from in the runtime, 2) KV cache / prefix caching effects, 3) batching behavior and latency windows, 4) quantization trade-offs, 5) deployment considerations (Dedicated / Private / VPC).
[00:52] Tom Becker: We'll probably run some benchmarks ourselves but want to validate assumptions. Also need to see differences between hosted API vs dedicated GPU pools vs private on-prem in terms of determinism.
[01:10] Priya Singh: One constraint on our side: on-prem infra cannot have outbound egress except to our KMS for key ops. That may limit telemetry; also need SOC2 audit proof.
[01:25] Ravi Patel: Noted. We'll touch on KMS integrations and audit logs later.
[01:30] Lena Morales: One quick baseline: current system uses OpenAI API for chat completions and a small internal function caller that parses JSON; typical payloads are 150-300 tokens. We care about both median and p95.
[01:46] Sofia Chen: Ok, good baseline. When using Redwood tool/function calling with JSON mode, there are two main sources of overhead vs plain text generation: constrained decoding enforcement and post-generation structured validation/repair. Constrained decoding increases compute per-step and sometimes reduces parallelism, so per-token latency can go up, often by 5-20% depending on model and implementation.
[02:15] Ravi Patel: To expand: constrained decoding means we either run a constrained beam/DP over token choices, or we apply per-token filtering on logits then sample. If you force exact-json grammar, we might use a separate constrained-decoder path which has extra checks at each step; that is slightly more CPU and memory work.
[02:35] Tom Becker: Is that mostly CPU on the host or extra GPU kernel time?
[02:40] Ravi Patel: Mostly a mix. The heavy token scoring still happens on GPU, but constrained decoding has additional small CPU loops to apply lexical constraints and sometimes re-encode partial tokens. For large batches this CPU cost amortizes, but for low-latency single requests it matters.
[02:58] Priya Singh: So for our 300ms SLA that could push us over for single-shot calls?
[03:02] Sofia Chen: Potentially, yes. That's where KV cache and prefix caching can help. If your prompts reuse long prefixes (system + few examples), the KV cache avoids re-computing key/value attention states for the prefix, reducing GPU work and latency significantly.
[03:18] Ravi Patel: Example numbers from our internal tests: with a 2k-token prefix and 200-token completion, a cold run on hosted API might be 650ms median on a mid-tier model; with KV cache warmed you can see 220-300ms depending on batch size and quantization. So caching is a big lever.
[03:41] Tom Becker: That matches intuition. Our prompts often reuse the same system prompt and 3 examples, so cacheable. How does tool calling interact with KV cache?
[03:50] Ravi Patel: Tool calling typically alters the decoding process but doesn't invalidate the KV cache for the prefix. The cache stores the transformer states up to the decode start. So as long as you start generation from the same prefix, tool calling constraints are applied during decoding but the prefix compute is reused.
[04:06] Lena Morales: What about when structured output requires us to include variable-length fields (like an array of items)? Does that cause retries and increase latency?
[04:13] Ravi Patel: If the structured constraints are strict (like matching a JSON schema), you can get partial repairs: the decoder may produce an invalid token and the constrained decoder then backtracks or applies correction heuristics. That can increase decode steps slightly — think a few extra token attempts, which translates to extra GPU decode iterations. In our measurements that's usually a small tail effect, but it depends on schema complexity.
[04:36] Priya Singh: Could we instead generate plain text and post-parse? Is that faster?
[04:41] Sofia Chen: Plain text then parse is often faster on median latency but increases post-processing cost and error rates. For AtlasPay, where correctness is important for downstream enrichment, constrained generation + validation reduces parsing failures. It's a classic speed vs correctness tradeoff.
[04:59] Tom Becker: Let's talk batching. We run a lot of small requests; how does Redwood's continuous batching affect tail SLOs?
[05:06] Ravi Patel: Our runtime uses adaptive batching windows. For low load, we prefer immediate single-request paths, but for better throughput we open micro-batches up to a configurable window (e.g., 10-50ms). Batching improves GPU utilization and lowers cost-per-token, but it adds queuing latency.
[05:24] Sofia Chen: For AtlasPay's p95 requirement, you can tune the batching target/timeout: set small max-wait (like 10ms) to keep p95 low, or use Dedicated where you get guaranteed concurrency and can set lower batch sizes. There's also per-customer routing policies so critical routes get a lower-batch fallback.
[05:42] Tom Becker: How deterministic is the Dedicated option? If we reserve GPU pools and avoid multi-tenant bursts, can we expect consistent p95?
[05:50] Ravi Patel: Dedicated reduces noisy neighbor effects and gives predictable throughput. We also offer burst capacity with guardrails. But constrained decoding overhead is algorithmic and will still affect per-token time; Dedicated just makes the baseline GPU time stable.
[06:05] Lena Morales: Great. Now quantization — we saw mentions of 8-bit and 4-bit. How does quantization affect constrained decoding and structured output quality?
[06:15] Ravi Patel: Quantization reduces model size and can improve throughput on certain runtimes but may introduce slight quality regression. For structured JSON, regressions can manifest as format errors or slightly worse token probabilities leading to more repairs. Our recommendation: test with per-workload evals. We provide quantization profiles per-model that balance speed and JSON robustness. For example, LLM-X 4-bit ocq gave 1.6x throughput with ~2-3% increase in parse errors on our evals.
[06:45] Priya Singh: Can Redwood run these quantized builds in our private VPC/on-prem?
[06:49] Ravi Patel: Yes, Private supports our runtime images with quantized kernels. On-prem comes with a validated image bundle; we run the same kernels but under your network and KMS. Note that some kernel optimizations require specific CUDA or driver versions — we'll validate those in the pilot.
[07:06] Tom Becker: About VPC and on-prem: telemetry and logs — we need audit logs but can't allow raw request data to leave network. How does Redwood handle audit and observability?
[07:17] Sofia Chen: For Private deployments we offer a control plane option that can be run inside customer network; logs can be stored locally to your SIEM and KMS-managed. For Hosted and Dedicated, we offer redaction options and enterprise retention controls. We also produce token-level cost/latency breakdowns but can send only aggregated metrics if you prefer no raw payload egress.
[07:38] Lena Morales: Good. Back to runtime specifics — you mentioned constrained-decoder path using per-token pruning. Any opportunities to accelerate that on the GPU side?
[07:48] Ravi Patel: There are a few: 1) push constraint checks into fused kernels (we're working on fused constrained-sampling kernels), 2) apply early prefix validation to reduce backtracking, and 3) use schema-guided templating where model only needs to fill specific fields rather than full JSON generation. Those reduce extra CPU loops and GPU round trips.
[08:12] Tom Becker: Schema-guided templating sounds promising — is that like generating values only and stitching into a known skeleton?
[08:18] Ravi Patel: Exactly. You send the skeleton e.g., {"items": [<GEN>], "score": <GEN>} and the model only generates inside markers. That significantly reduces constrained search space and improves latency/robustness.
[08:31] Priya Singh: Any differences for streaming responses vs non-streaming when generating JSON?
[08:37] Ravi Patel: Streaming plus JSON constraints is trickier: you need to ensure partial outputs don't break the schema for the consumer. We often recommend streaming with checkpoints or streaming only once validated chunks are available. Streaming does reduce time-to-first-byte but may increase complexity for structured validation.
[08:56] Sofia Chen: Also note our console can show token-level latency and fallback counts so you can correlate when constrained decode incurred backtracks.
[09:05] Lena Morales: Can you walk us through the benchmark plan you suggested?
[09:09] Ravi Patel: We'll run three scenarios: 1) Hosted baseline (your prompt set, default model, quantization off), 2) Dedicated (reserved GPUs, same model and quantization), 3) Private on-prem image (your infra). For each: measure median, p95, and parse error rate for JSON outputs, plus cost per 1k tokens. We'll also instrument KV cache warm vs cold.
[09:34] Tom Becker: For KV cache we need a way to pre-warm caches for continuous traffic. Any suggestions?
[09:40] Ravi Patel: You can pre-warm by replaying representative prefixes or using a caching hint API we provide. For Dedicated you can configure persistent session caches for pinned model versions. Private supports persistence too but you'll manage cache lifecycle.
[09:52] Priya Singh: On the topic of SSO/KMS, what auth flows does Private support?
[09:57] Sofia Chen: Private can integrate with SAML/SSO for console access, and KMS via customer-managed keys (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HSM). We can also support Bring-Your-Own-HSM in the on-prem package.
[10:12] Lena Morales: Ok sounds good. A couple more nitty-gritty: what about tokenization differences causing JSON token boundaries that make constrained decoding harder?
[10:22] Ravi Patel: Yes — tokenization irregularities near braces/quotes can increase invalid token emissions. We mitigate with token-level post-processing heuristics and by recommending schema choices that avoid producing punctuation-heavy structures when possible. Also using byte-level tokens or different tokenizer variants can help.
[10:40] Tom Becker: Can we get an example config for constrained decoding and batching?
[10:45] Ravi Patel: Yes, I'll attach config snippets after the call — includes max-batch-wait, max-batch-size, constrained-decoder: {mode: json-schema, repair: true, max-backtracks: 3} and quantization profile references.
[10:59] Sofia Chen: Quick objection that sometimes comes up from procurement — constrained decoding and dedicated options sound expensive. How do you recommend minimizing cost?
[11:07] Ravi Patel: Use hybrid routing: route percentage of traffic through cheaper quantized models with post-parse validation and fall back to higher-quality model on failures. Also cache aggressively and use batching during peak windows. Redwood Optimize has suggestions to tune these automatically.
[11:24] Lena Morales: That sounds like a practical approach.
[11:28] Priya Singh: Any legal notes we should be aware of for on-prem images?
[11:31] Sofia Chen: The on-prem image is shipped under our enterprise agreement. We include a manifest of included binaries and licensing terms. We'll coordinate with your legal.
[11:41] Tom Becker: Back to performance numbers — can you share recent internal numbers for JSON-mode p95 with and without quantization?
[11:48] Ravi Patel: Example (approx): Model A, hosted, json-mode, no quant: median 260ms p95 520ms parse-fail 1.8%. Model A, dedicated, quant 8-bit: median 170ms p95 330ms parse-fail 2.6%. Model A, dedicated, 4-bit: median 120ms p95 420ms parse-fail 5.2% (higher parse errors). These are illustrative; we'll run your prompts for accurate numbers.
[12:18] Lena Morales: Ok that's helpful. The 4-bit parse error rate is a concern.
[12:22] Ravi Patel: Hence the test matrix. We can also try mixed precision where code paths keep certain layers in higher precision to improve quality.
[12:33] Priya Singh: For the pilot, what telemetry will Redwood need? We prefer not to share raw PII or full payloads.
[12:40] Sofia Chen: For the pilot we only need the prompts and a mapping of user IDs (can be hashed). Redwood can run benchmarks in your VPC or on Dedicated with local logs. We'll agree to a data handling Addendum.
[12:55] Tom Becker: Great. Anything else on constrained decoding we should be aware of?
[12:59] Ravi Patel: One more: when schema is very deep (nested arrays/objects) the constrained search tree grows. Using skeleton templating or generating compact canonical forms helps. Also consider post-generation deterministic normalizers.
[13:16] Lena Morales: Good. Let's confirm action items and timelines.
[13:20] Sofia Chen: Recap: we'll send benchmark template, config snippets, and pricing. AtlasPay will give prompt set and confirm infra constraints. We'll run pilot week of 2026-03-16 pending infra validation.
[13:33] Priya Singh: I'll validate on-prem driver versions and KMS endpoints and send to Ravi.
[13:38] Tom Becker: I'll assemble the prompt set by the 10th.
[13:42] Sofia Chen: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the artifacts.
[13:49] Lena Morales: Thanks all.

[57:00] (end)
